title: Data Engineering for ML: Streaming and Spark
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Data Engineering for ML: Streaming and Spark ##### The fraud model that was always 40 minutes late A payments company in Mumbai ran a fraud model whose features came from a Spark batch job executing every 30 minutes. Adding job runtime, the freshest feature a scoring request could see was about 40 minutes old. Card-testing fraud works in bursts. An attacker validates stolen card numbers with dozens of small transactions in eight to twelve minutes, then moves on. By the time `txns_last_15min` was computed and loaded, the attack was over and the money was gone. The fix was not a better model. It was a Kafka consumer maintaining a windowed counter in Redis, giving the model a feature that was 200 milliseconds old instead of 40 minutes. Detection rate on burst fraud went from 11% to 74%. The lesson generalises: **feature freshness is a modelling decision, and it is decided by your data architecture.** Choosing batch when you needed streaming caps your model's ceiling before you write a line of training code. ##### Batch vs streaming | | Batch | Streaming | |---|---|---| | Latency | Minutes to hours | Milliseconds to seconds | | Data view | Complete, bounded window | Incomplete, unbounded | | Reprocessing | Trivial — rerun the job | Hard — replay from the log | | Correctness | Easy; all data present | Hard; late and out-of-order events | | Cost | Lower per record | Higher (always-on) | | Debugging | Straightforward | Genuinely difficult | | Good for | Training sets, daily aggregates, backfills | Fraud, personalisation, anomaly detection | The honest decision rule: **use batch unless the business value decays within minutes.** Streaming infrastructure costs roughly 3–5× more in engineering time and operational burden. Most "real-time" requirements dissolve under questioning — a recommendation refreshed hourly is usually indistinguishable from one refreshed per second. But when freshness genuinely matters — fraud, dynamic pricing, live personalisation, anomaly detection on telemetry — no amount of model quality compensates for stale features. ##### PySpark for batch feature engineering Spark's model: partition data across a cluster, apply transformations lazily to build a DAG, and execute only when an action demands results. The Catalyst optimiser rewrites your query before anything runs. ```python from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, Window spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("fraud-features") .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") # AQE: fixes skew at runtime .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "400") .config("spark.serializer", "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer") .getOrCreate()) txns = (spark.read.format("delta").load("s3://lake/silver/transactions") .filter(F.col("txn_date").between("2026-01-01", "2026-06-30")) # partition pruning .select("user_id", "txn_ts", "amount_inr", "merchant_id", "city", "is_fraud")) # Point-in-time-correct rolling features: rangeBetween on a UNIX timestamp w7 = (Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy(F.col("ts_unix")) .rangeBetween(-7 * 86400, -1)) # ends at -1 second: excludes current row w30 = (Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy(F.col("ts_unix")) .rangeBetween(-30 * 86400, -1)) features = (txns .withColumn("ts_unix", F.col("txn_ts").cast("long")) .withColumn("amt_avg_7d", F.avg("amount_inr").over(w7)) .withColumn("amt_std_30d", F.stddev("amount_inr").over(w30)) .withColumn("txn_count_7d", F.count("*").over(w7)) .withColumn("distinct_merchants_30d", F.size(F.collect_set("merchant_id").over(w30))) .withColumn("amt_zscore", (F.col("amount_inr") - F.col("amt_avg_7d")) / F.when(F.col("amt_std_30d") > 0, F.col("amt_std_30d")).otherwise(F.lit(None))) .withColumn("hour_ist", F.hour(F.from_utc_timestamp("txn_ts", "Asia/Kolkata"))) .withColumn("is_night", (F.col("hour_ist") < 6).cast("int")) ) (features.repartition("txn_date") .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") .partitionBy("txn_date").option("overwriteSchema", "true") .save("s3://lake/gold/fraud_features")) ``` The `rangeBetween(-7*86400, -1)` ending at −1 is the leakage guard: the current row is excluded from its own rolling window. In a distributed engine this is easy to get wrong and impossible to spot later. Performance issues in Spark are almost always **shuffles and skew**. A shuffle redistributes data across the network — triggered by `groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, `repartition`, and window functions with a partition key. Skew happens when one key dominates: if 40% of transactions belong to one aggregator merchant, that partition's task runs 40× longer than the rest while every other executor idles. Fixes, in order: enable **Adaptive Query Execution** (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled`), which splits skewed partitions automatically; **broadcast join** small dimension tables (`F.broadcast(dim_df)`) so no shuffle occurs; and **salt** the key as a last resort — append a random suffix to distribute a hot key, aggregate, then re-aggregate. Two more rules: prefer built-in `pyspark.sql.functions` over Python UDFs, because UDFs serialise every row between the JVM and a Python process (a 10–100× penalty); when you must use Python, use **Pandas UDFs** (`@pandas_udf`), which operate on Arrow batches and are vastly faster. And `df.cache()` before reusing a DataFrame multiple times, because Spark otherwise recomputes the whole lineage each time. ##### Streaming: Kafka and processing semantics Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, append-only log. Producers write to topics; consumers read at their own offset. Because the log is durable and replayable, you can reprocess history — which is what makes it the backbone of streaming ML. The concepts that determine correctness: **Event time vs processing time.** An event occurred at 10:02:15 (event time) but arrived at 10:04:41 (processing time), because a phone was in a tunnel. Aggregating by processing time gives wrong answers. Always window on event time. **Watermarks** bound how long you wait for stragglers: "process the window once the watermark passes; anything later is dropped or sent to a side output." A 10-minute watermark trades correctness against latency, and choosing it is a business decision. **Delivery semantics.** *At-most-once* may lose events. *At-least-once* may duplicate them. *Exactly-once* requires idempotent writes plus transactional offset commits. For counting features, duplicates directly corrupt the value — so exactly-once, or idempotent sinks, matter. ```python from pyspark.sql import functions as F from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StringType, DoubleType, TimestampType schema = (StructType() .add("user_id", StringType()).add("amount_inr", DoubleType()) .add("merchant_id", StringType()).add("event_time", TimestampType())) stream = (spark.readStream.format("kafka") .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS) .option("subscribe", "transactions") .option("startingOffsets", "latest") .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 200_000) # backpressure .load() .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("d")).select("d.*")) windowed = (stream .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes") # tolerate 10 min lateness .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "15 minutes", "1 minute"), F.col("user_id")) .agg(F.count("*").alias("txn_count_15m"), F.sum("amount_inr").alias("amount_15m"), F.approx_count_distinct("merchant_id").alias("merchants_15m"))) (windowed.writeStream .outputMode("update") .foreachBatch(lambda df, epoch: upsert_to_redis(df, epoch)) # idempotent sink .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake/checkpoints/fraud-features") .trigger(processingTime="10 seconds") .start()) ``` The `checkpointLocation` is what makes the stream fault-tolerant — it stores offsets and aggregation state so a restart resumes exactly where it stopped. Never delete it casually, and never point two streams at the same one. **Flink** is the alternative worth knowing: true event-at-a-time processing (Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch), lower latency, and richer state management with the `KeyedProcessFunction` API. Choose Spark when your team already knows it and 1–10 second latency suffices; choose Flink when you need sub-second latency or complex event-time state machines. ##### Lakehouse: Delta Lake Data lakes gave cheap storage and no guarantees — no atomicity, no schema enforcement, no time travel. The lakehouse adds a transaction log over Parquet and gets all three back. ```python from delta.tables import DeltaTable # ACID upsert (MERGE) — impossible with plain Parquet tgt = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, "s3://lake/gold/user_features") (tgt.alias("t").merge(updates.alias("s"), "t.user_id = s.user_id") .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()) # Time travel: reproduce exactly the training data used in March march = spark.read.format("delta").option("timestampAsOf", "2026-03-15").load(PATH) v42 = spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 42).load(PATH) spark.sql("OPTIMIZE delta.`s3://lake/gold/user_features` ZORDER BY (user_id)") spark.sql("VACUUM delta.`s3://lake/gold/user_features` RETAIN 720 HOURS") ``` **Time travel is the reproducibility answer for ML.** `versionAsOf 42` in your training config means "the March model" is exactly recoverable, forever — which is precisely what the audit scenario from the pipelines day demanded. The medallion pattern organises the lake: **bronze** (raw, append-only, immutable), **silver** (cleaned, deduplicated, typed, validated), **gold** (aggregated, model-ready features). Each layer is reproducible from the one above. ##### Data quality at scale ```python from pyspark.sql import functions as F EXPECTATIONS = { "amount_positive": F.col("amount_inr") > 0, "amount_bounded": F.col("amount_inr") < 10_000_000, "user_id_present": F.col("user_id").isNotNull(), "ts_not_future": F.col("txn_ts") <= F.current_timestamp(), "city_known": F.col("city").isin(KNOWN_CITIES), } def enforce(df, expectations, fail_threshold=0.01, quarantine_path=None): n = df.count() cond = F.lit(True) for name, expr in expectations.items(): failures = df.filter(~expr).count() rate = failures / max(n, 1) METRIC.labels(check=name).set(rate) if rate > fail_threshold: raise ValueError(f"{name}: {rate:.2%} failed (> {fail_threshold:.0%})") cond = cond & expr if quarantine_path: df.filter(~cond).write.format("delta").mode("append").save(quarantine_path) return df.filter(cond) ``` The **quarantine** pattern matters at scale: bad rows are written aside rather than dropped silently, so you can inspect what broke and reprocess after fixing the source. Silent filtering is how a 3% data loss goes unnoticed for a quarter. ##### Unifying batch and streaming: the skew problem returns ```mermaid flowchart TD K[Kafka: transaction events] --> S[Streaming job: 15-min windows] K --> L[Bronze Delta: raw append] S --> R[(Redis online store
fresh, seconds old)] L --> B[Spark batch: silver + gold] B --> O[(Delta offline store
complete, point-in-time)] O -->|historical features| T[Training] R -->|online features| I[Inference] T --> M[Model] M --> I P[Parity job: recompute a sample
offline, diff against logged online] --> A{Match?} R -.sampled.-> P O -.-> P A -->|No| AL[Alert: training/serving skew] ``` Two paths computing "the same" feature is exactly the training/serving skew problem, now with two different engines and two different languages. Three mitigations, in order of strength: 1. **One definition, two runtimes.** Express features once (SQL, or a feature-store definition) and compile to both paths. This is what Feast, Tecton and Chronon exist to do. 2. **Kappa architecture.** Drop the batch path entirely; generate training data by replaying the Kafka log through the *same* streaming code. Elegant, and demanding of retention and compute. 3. **A parity job.** Recompute a daily sample of logged online features through the offline path and alert on any mismatch beyond tolerance. Whatever else you do, do this — it is cheap and it catches everything. ##### Common mistakes - Building streaming infrastructure for a use case where hourly batch was sufficient. - Windowing on processing time instead of event time. - No watermark, so state grows without bound until the job OOMs. - Python UDFs in a hot Spark path instead of built-ins or Pandas UDFs. - Ignoring skew and blaming Spark for a job where one task runs 40× longer. - Rolling windows that include the current row. - Deleting or sharing a streaming checkpoint directory. - Plain Parquet where you needed ACID upserts and time travel. - Dropping invalid rows silently instead of quarantining them. - Two implementations of one feature, with no parity check. ##### Hands-on Build a PySpark batch feature pipeline over a large dataset with leakage-safe windowed aggregations, written to partitioned Delta with `ZORDER`. Deliberately introduce a skewed key, observe the straggler task in the Spark UI, and fix it with AQE or salting — record the before-and-after runtime. Then prototype a streaming job consuming from Kafka with event-time windows, a watermark, and an idempotent Redis sink. For the mini-project, build a lambda-style pipeline: a Spark batch path producing point-in-time-correct training features into Delta, a streaming path producing fresh online features into Redis, data-quality enforcement with quarantine on both, and a daily parity job that recomputes a sample and alerts on mismatch. Demonstrate reproducibility by training from `versionAsOf` a specific Delta version. Then write your batch-versus-streaming explanation with a concrete use case that genuinely requires streaming — the card-testing burst above is the archetype, and the numbers make the argument. ##### Key takeaways - Feature freshness caps model quality; choose batch or streaming from how fast the business value decays, not from fashion. - Spark performance is shuffles and skew — enable AQE, broadcast small joins, and avoid Python UDFs in hot paths. - Stream correctness is event time plus watermarks plus idempotent sinks; processing-time windows quietly produce wrong features. - Delta Lake's ACID transactions and time travel are what make lake-based ML reproducible and auditable. - Two paths computing one feature will diverge — unify the definition, and run a parity check regardless.
